item.title: Will Republicans or Democrats win the Senate? These key midterm races will decide.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Control of both chambers of Congress is up for grabs in November's election. But as important as the House of Representatives is, all signs point to the true drama of the midterms being in the battle for the Senate. There are 35 Senate seats on the ballot this year. Most of those races won't be competitive. The balance of power in the Senate will be decided by the dozen or so states where the outcome truly is uncertain. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority, which means they can lose three seats and still maintain control of the chamber — thanks to Vice President JD Vance's constitutionally granted power to break ties in an evenly split Senate. Forecasters widely expect Democrats to flip the House, but view the Senate as a "true toss-up." The key Senate battlegrounds include traditional swing states, idiosyncratic areas of the Northeast and historically Republican states where Democrats have rarely been competitive in recent elections. The outcome will have enormous implications for the final two years of President Trump's tenure in the White House. Democrats only need to gain control of one chamber to have the power to block or reshape Trump's legislative agenda. But a Senate majority would empower them to do much more. They would have an effective veto over Trump's nominees for high-ranking Cabinet positions and could block him from appointing any new Supreme Court justices. Control over key Senate committees would also allow Democrats to launch sweeping investigations into Trump and his administration. Here's a rundown of the races that will likely decide which party controls the Senate after the midterms. Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola and Republican Dan Sullivan Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Amanda Andrade-Rhoades/AP, Greg Nash/Pool via Reuters Party control : GOP The Republican : Dan Sullivan The Democrat : Mary Peltola True to the state's image, there's a wildness to Alaska's Senate race that you won't find elsewhere in the country. On paper, incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan should be well-positioned to win a third term in the Senate. Alaska is a consistently red state that has only elected a Democrat to the Senate once in the past 45 years. Democrats' challenges in the state have been so acute recently that they didn't even have a candidate on the ballot the last time Sullivan was up for reelection. Yahoo But forecasters expect this year's race to be much closer. Sullivan's main opponent is former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola , who was Alaska's lone member of the House from 2022 to 2025. Peltola, the first Alaska Native and first woman to represent the Last Frontier in Congress, is a rare Democrat with a record of success in statewide elections. Sen. Sullivan's path to reelection is also complicated by the presence of a long-shot candidate who shares his name, Dan J. Sullivan, who will also appear on the ballot — potentially creating confusion over which Sullivan voters intend to support. Florida Democrat Angie Nixon and Republican Ashley Moody Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Joe Raedle/Getty Images, Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images Party control : GOP The Republican : Ashley Moody The Democrat : Angie Nixon It would likely take a major blue wave election for incumbent Republican Sen. Ashley Moody to be at a real risk of being unseated by progressive Democrat Angie Nixon. The GOP has won the last two Senate races in Florida by an average of 14 points. Polls have shown Nixon trailing by a smaller margin than that, but still far enough behind for forecasters to rate the race as favoring Republicans. Georgia Democrat Jon Ossoff and Republican Mike Collins Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Brynn Anderson/AP, Jason Allen/Getty Images Party control : Democratic The Republican : Mike Collins The Democrat : Jon Ossoff On top of flipping a handful of GOP-held seats, Democrats' chances of gaining control of the Senate rely on keeping the ones they already have. One of the most important is in Georgia. Sen. Jon Ossoff became a rising star within the Democratic Party when he pulled off a stunning upset in the 2020 elections, defeating incumbent Republican David Perdue in an extremely tight runoff. Ossoff is now running for reelection for the first time. His opponent is Rep. Mike Collins, a MAGA-friendly congressman who has created controversy with a series of divisive social media posts during his tenure in the House. More recently, Collins has faced intense scrutiny over his social media posts and the online activity of people close to him , including his son-in-law . Polls have shown Ossoff with a healthy lead over Collins, enough of a gap that forecasters at the non-partisan Center for Politics wrote in July that it would be a "true shock" if he isn't reelected. Iowa Democrat Josh Turek and Republican Ashley Hinson Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Scott Olson/Getty Images, Charlie Neibergall/Getty Images Party control : GOP The Republican : Ashley Hinson The Democrat : Josh Turek It wasn't that long ago that Iowa was viewed as one of the country's quintessential swing states, but the Hawkeye State has shifted significantly to the right over the past decade — to the point where it's no longer competitive in presidential elections. That said, polls suggest Democrats appear to have a real chance of flipping the Senate seat held by retiring incumbent Joni Ernst. Their nominee is Josh Turek, a state lawmaker and two-time Paralympic gold medalist. A moderate who describes himself as a "prairie populist," Turek has focused heavily on how Trump's tariffs and the war with Iran have affected farmers in his state throughout the campaign. His opponent is GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson, a former local news anchor who cruised to the Republican nomination after earning Trump's endorsement. Polling of the race has fluctuated significantly, with both candidates showing small leads at different times. Kansas Democrat Adam Hamilton and Republican Roger Marshall Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Emily Curiel/The Kansas City Star/Tribune News Service via Getty Images, Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images Party control : GOP The Republican : Roger Marshall The Democrat : Adam Hamilton It has been almost 100 years since Kansas elected a Democrat to the Senate, but the state may be in play this year as incumbent Republican Roger Marshall looks to keep the GOP's nearly century-long winning streak alive. His opponent is Adam Hamilton, a pastor and the founder of the nation's largest United Methodist church. Forecasters are split on whether Marshall is still the favorite to win, or if the race should be considered a toss-up . Either way, the outcome looks to be on track to be much closer than Republicans are used to in the Sunflower State. Independent voters have favored Hamilton by a large margin in recent surveys. Libertarian Party candidate David Graham is also on the ballot and has drawn a small but potentially significant share of support in some polls. Maine Democrat Troy Jackson and Republican Susan Collins Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Robert F. Bukaty/AP, Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images Party control : GOP The Republican : Susan Collins The Democrat : Troy Jackson Democrats have been eyeing Sen. Susan Collins's seat for decades, but the Republican has fended off every challenger they've sent her way during her 30 years in the Senate. Her opponent this time around will be Troy Jackson , a former logger and longtime member of the state legislature. Jackson was chosen at a hastily planned convention after the party's original nominee, Graham Platner, dropped out of the race following an allegation of sexual assault, which he denied, among other controversies. Collins has historically managed to outperform other Republicans when she's been on the ballot, even in "blue wave" years like 2020, in part because of her longstanding reputation as a relative moderate within her party. But that image is being tested in this race. Jackson has centered much of his campaign on tying Collins to some of the more high-profile times she's sided with the president on major issues, particularly her votes to confirm Supreme Court justices who later joined the majority in overturning Roe v. Wade . Jackson faces his own challenges. He is playing catch-up after becoming the nominee so late in the process. He will also face scrutiny over his past conservative positions on issues like abortion and same-sex marriage, which are a far cry from the progressive political views he expresses today. Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Slaven Vlasic/Getty Images, Jeff Kowalsky/AFP via Getty Images Party control : Democratic The Republican : Mike Rogers The Democrat : Abdul El-Sayed One of the nation's few genuine swing states is home to one of the most pivotal midterm matchups. Incumbent Democrat Gary Peters opted not to run for a third term, setting the stage for a nailbiter of a Democratic primary in which progressive physician Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens, a relative moderate, in a major victory for the party's left wing. There was far less drama on the Republican side, where former Rep. Mike Rogers cruised to the GOP nomination. Rogers was also the Republican nominee in 2024, losing to Democrat Elissa Slotkin by 0.34 percentage points of the vote in one of the tightest Senate races in the country. El-Sayed, who supports policies like a billionaire's tax and Medicare for All, will need the support of centrist Democrats and swing voters in order to build a big enough coalition to win what polls suggest could be another extremely close general election. Minnesota Democrat Peggy Flanagan and Republican Michele Tafoya Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Abbie Parr/AP, Ellen Schmidt/AP Party control : Democratic The Republican : Michele Tafoya The Democrat : Peggy Flanagan Incumbent Sen. Tina Smith has opted not to run for a second term, which could help create an opening for Republicans to break Democrats' longstanding hold on Minnesota's U.S. Senate delegation. To pursue that goal, the GOP has enlisted a rare political newcomer with widespread name recognition: Former sports broadcaster Michele Tafoya. Her Democratic opponent is Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan. The race so far has been defined by the remarkably different approaches of the two candidates. Tafoya has worked to push her party toward the political center, portraying herself as a moderate Republican and mostly focusing on issues like affordability and public safety while steering clear of some of the more divisive parts of Trump's agenda. Flanagan, on the other hand, is a progressive who represents a significant step to the left on policy for Democrats relative to Smith. Polls have suggested that the race could be extremely close . Nebraska Independent Dan Osborn and Republican Pete Ricketts Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images, Alex Brandon/AP Party control : GOP The Republican : Pete Ricketts The independent : Dan Osborn In a state as red as Nebraska, rather than fielding their own candidate to challenge incumbent Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts, Democrats have thrown their support behind independent candidate Dan Osborn. This is the second time that Osborn, a Navy veteran and former labor union leader, has run for the Senate in a race without a Democratic candidate. Two years ago, he finished about 6 points behind GOP Sen. Deb Fisher in the state's closest Senate race in more than two decades. Osborn has been deeply critical of both parties and says he opposes parts of the Democratic Party's platform. But if he's elected, the GOP would lose a Senate seat it currently holds and one vote that it can comfortably count on in support of Trump's legislative agenda. New Hampshire Democrat Chris Pappas and Republican John E. Sununu Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images, Sophie Park/Getty Images Party control : Democratic The Republican : John Sununu The Democrat : Chris Pappas The Granite State is rarely discussed as a swing state because it consistently votes for Democrats in presidential elections. But Senate races are a different story. Several Republicans have been elected to represent New Hampshire in the Senate in recent decades. One of them is John Sununu, who is running to regain the seat he lost in 2008 when he was defeated by Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, the retiring incumbent. Sununu is part of a political dynasty in the state. His father, also named John, and his brother Chris both served as governor. The Democratic nominee is Rep. Chris Pappas, a moderate who comfortably outpaced a democratic socialist rival in his party's primary. Pappas is the first gay man to represent New Hampshire in Congress and would become the first openly gay male senator in U.S. history if he is elected. North Carolina Democrat Roy Cooper and Republican Michael Whatley Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Allen G. Breed/AP, Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images Party control : GOP The Republican : Michael Whatley The Democrat : Roy Cooper If polls are accurate, Republicans have a lot of ground to make up if they want to hold on to this seat from the Tarheel State. Incumbent Sen. Thom Tillis, a rare member of the GOP caucus to defy the president in some circumstances, has opted not to seek reelection. The Republican nominee to replace him is Michael Whatley, a former chair of the Republican National Committee. Whatley has a strong history in North Carolina, having run the state Republican Party for nearly five years, but he lacks the statewide name recognition of his Democratic opponent, former Gov. Roy Cooper. Both of Cooper's gubernatorial wins were reasonably close, but polls have shown him with a significant lead over Whatley. Forecasters have also shifted the race toward Democrats. Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown and Republican Jon Husted Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Jeff Dean/AP, Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Party control : GOP The Republican : Jon Husted The Democrat : Sherrod Brown The Buckeye State has trended to the right over the past decade or so, but a unique set of circumstances has contributed to making this race a genuine toss-up in the eyes of some forecasters. Aside from the Democratic and Republican nominees, Libertarian William Redpath and Greg Levy of the Party for Socialism and Liberation are also on the ballot. These two lesser-known candidates are getting as much as 6% of voters' support in polls, collectively, which is potentially enough to influence the outcome in a very tight race. Husted is the rare incumbent with less experience than his challenger. He has only been in the Senate since 2025, when he was appointed to fill the vacancy created when JD Vance became vice president. Brown, on the other hand, served three full terms in the Senate before losing his seat to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024. Brown also has a massive cash advantage, which has allowed his campaign to spend more than four times as much as Husted's so far, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Despite all of that, Brown is still swimming upstream in a state that has become solidly red over the past few election cycles. South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews and Republican Darline Graham Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Sean Rayford/Getty Images Party control : GOP The Republican : Darline Graham The Democrat : Annie Andrews The word "competitive" is rarely used to describe statewide races in a place as red as South Carolina, but the death of longtime incumbent Sen. Lindsey Graham in July has set up what could be the Palmetto State's first tight Senate race in a generation. Graham's sister, Darline Graham, was appointed to finish the rest of his term and is now running for a full six-year term. Her opponent is Democrat Annie Andrews, a pediatrician who has staked out several policy positions that reflect the state's conservatism, including support for the Second Amendment, tax cuts and strong immigration enforcement. Republicans have comfortably won every Senate election in South Carolina since the early 2000s, but Trump's declining approval rating in the state and apparent concerns about Graham's lack of experience have likely contributed to making this a much closer race. Recent polls have shown Andrews trailing by as little as a single point, though forecasters still list the state as a likely Republican victory. Texas Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Brenda Bazán/AP, Tony Gutierrez/AP Party control : GOP The Republican : Ken Paxton The Democrat : James Talarico Republicans haven't lost a statewide election in the Lone Star State in more than three decades, but forecasters say Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico has a chance of ending that streak in November. His Republican opponent is Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who defeated longtime incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in a tightly contested and often contentious Republican primary. Paxton has faced serious legal issues during his tenure as Texas's top law enforcement official, including accusations of corruption that led the state House to impeach him in 2023. The state Senate later acquitted him on all articles it considered. Polls have consistently shown a tight contest , with a good number finding Talarico leading by a small margin. item.title: House speaker's wife ministers to Hill staffers, but nonprofit funding is a mystery
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
After House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana) ascended to one of the most powerful offices in Washington three years ago, his wife, a faith-based counselor, turned her focus to the nation’s capital. Kelly Johnson reoriented a religious nonprofit she was running back home in the Shreveport area into a ministry focused on female congressional staffers. Its new purpose, according to an IRS filing, was to help “the hundreds of unreached young women” working around Capitol Hill “find purpose, belonging, and Christian community.” Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Through the organization, a part-time endeavor run solely by Johnson, she provides counseling, delivers speeches and conducts “spiritual heritage tours” of the U.S. Capitol that highlight the nation’s Christian history. In 2024, financial disclosures show Johnson was paid $50,000 for 10 hours of work per week. The nonprofit, Onward Christian Education Services, has become part of the rising presence in official Washington of evangelical Christianity as its devotees, a key bloc of support for President Donald Trump, seek to inject a biblical worldview into American politics and government. The centerpiece of Johnson’s organization is the faith-based counseling that she said she provides free to staff and the spouses of House members. “I’m a missionary here,” Johnson said in an interview. “It’s kind of a calling in this life for me,” she added. “This is what I love to do. This is my heart.” The full extent of Kelly Johnson’s work in Washington is unclear, however. Some mysteries remain about her organization, including who is funding it. Onward Christian Education Services brought in an average of more than $60,000 in contributions annually during its early years. Donors are disclosed to the IRS but redacted in publicly available filings. Johnson said her nonprofit has “several large benefactors,” whom she described as “primarily just individuals who have an interest in this and have a heart in this.” She would not name them or disclose whether they are also supporters of her husband’s political campaigns, and she declined to voluntarily provide unredacted filings to The Washington Post. The publicly available records contain inconsistencies and omissions. Johnson, who IRS filings indicate also does the bookkeeping, has occasionally revised annual revenue figures for previous years without explanation. On a 2023 annual form, she neglected to report her own salary, which accounts for almost 90 percent of spending since the organization formed. The Post spoke to four people who work on nonprofit law and government ethics. They stressed there’s nothing wrong with the purpose of Onward Christian Education Services but raised concerns about how Kelly Johnson’s close connection to the speaker’s office could benefit the nonprofit. “It should make everyone uncomfortable that the speaker’s wife would be raising money for a mission to serve congressional staff,” said Meredith McGehee, a former lobbyist for several nonpartisan groups that advocate for campaign finance transparency and anti-corruption measures in government. “It really dances on that blurred line of separation of church and state and using public resources for private interests.” In a statement, Mike Johnson praised his wife’s ministry work and Christian counseling services as life-changing for many. “She has a true gift with people and has inspired many other women to live out their faith, overcome their obstacles, and find peace and success, even in an environment as challenging as Capitol Hill,” he said. Kelly Johnson has intentionally tried to keep her nonprofit’s second chapter out of the spotlight after what she considered an unfairly hostile reception to the couple’s religious views when Mike Johnson became speaker in October 2023. Onward Christian Education Services previously operated for five years in Louisiana. The Post discovered the change in mission when a reporter requested recent IRS filings for the group, which had not filed legally required disclosures for tax-exempt organizations for two years. Kelly Johnson submitted the organization’s 2024 filing after the inquiry, revealing its new purpose, though she did not explain the delay. A spokesperson said Johnson requested an extension for her 2025 IRS filing and has not yet completed it. The form is typically due in May and nonprofits can ask for a six-month extension. After an initial interview, Johnson declined to speak to a reporter again. The Post has pieced together this portrait of Onward Christian Education Services through that conversation, an analysis of available public documents and written questions submitted to Mike Johnson’s office. The Johnsons were ordained as Southern Baptist missionaries more than two decades ago, and in 2017, their church in Benton, Louisiana, formally ordained Kelly Johnson as a minister. The same year, she was licensed as a pastoral counselor through the National Christian Counselors Association, opening a practice at the church. Though she has never held elected office herself, Johnson has also long been politically active. Two decades ago, when Mike Johnson was still a practicing attorney, the couple were vocal advocates for covenant marriage, a legal union with more limited standing for divorce, and participated in an interview with Diane Sawyer about their experience. Kelly Johnson has previously worked for Louisiana Right to Life, an antiabortion advocacy group. She was intimately involved in her husband’s political rise. In 2022, the couple started a podcast together covering “hot topics and current events from a Christian perspective,” which they hosted until Mike Johnson became speaker. Onward Christian Education Services was created as a tax-exempt organization in April 2019 to counter what the Johnsons described at the time as cultural attacks against people of faith and the traditional family. Kelly Johnson recently told The Post she came to see that education was important. “People have forgotten our history and our Christian heritage,” she said. “For a long time, I felt that burden.” The purpose of the nonprofit, according to early tax filings, was to “empower Christians to follow the Biblical commands to understand and meet the challenges of our day,” primarily through live seminars at churches across Louisiana and eventually other states. Kelly Johnson served as the CEO and the only employee. “Mike and Kelly Johnson ‘rang the bell’ to awaken our people to become Christian patriots,” Gevan Spinney, a local pastor who serves as president of Onward Christian Education Services’ board, told the Baptist Message, a faith-based publication, in an article that May touting the seminar. Onward Christian Education Services initially did not submit any filings to the IRS. In 2022, when Kelly Johnson submitted forms for the first three years of operation, she blamed “a communication gap and misunderstanding of the filing requirements” for a nonprofit so closely affiliated with a religious denomination. The organization paid $6,475 in penalties to the Treasury Department. From 2019 to 2023, Johnson reported working 10 hours a week for Onward Christian Education Services, earning between $35,383 and $64,485 annually. During the covid-19 pandemic, the organization developed prerecorded presentations of its seminars. The Johnsons’ podcast followed. Once her husband became speaker, Kelly Johnson said, the couple had to spend more time in Washington and were no longer able to conduct regular church visits. So in 2024, she transitioned the focus of her nonprofit to the capital, folding in her counseling business and offering free sessions. Johnson said she has 10 or 11 clients, whom she counsels through a lens of spirituality and the Bible about the issues that women face, including anxiety and depression, adjusting to a new city and problems with their families. The organization maintains a low profile because, Johnson said, she fears for her safety. Her clients come through word of mouth, rather than advertising, Johnson said, and unlike in Louisiana, where she had an office at her church, they meet for counseling sessions at home or over FaceTime. “People want things to be private,” she said. “If I had an office, there would likely be protesters outside of it. I would like to have an office. Boy, would I like to.” Taylor Haulsee, a spokesman for Mike Johnson, said in a statement that “no House Republican Caucus or member office has ever been used for” outreach to staffers and that most of the nonprofit’s activities take place away from the Capitol complex. Other programming since Onward Christian Education Services shifted to Washington has included Kelly Johnson speaking at a Christian women’s conference in Kentucky in 2024, leading the spiritual heritage tours of the Capitol and organizing a Bible study, which Johnson said was hard to maintain because “people are just so overcommitted.” Johnson turned down a request from The Post for one of her Capitol tours. Haulsee said the tours are within House guidelines and they are “scheduled for small groups of people upon request, which is the same access available to any and all citizens to the People’s House.” He would not share who those people are or what they visit on the tours. As she expanded her ministry into Washington, Johnson teamed up with “like-minded organizations operating in the nation’s capital such as Concerned Women for America, Inc.,” according to the 2024 IRS filing. Concerned Women for America is an advocacy group “dedicated to impacting the culture for Christ through education and public policy,” according to its website. A spokesperson declined to answer questions about the organization’s work with Johnson. Government ethics advocates said the lack of transparency surrounding Onward Christian Education Services means the public cannot be certain whether donors are using the organization to gain access to the Johnsons or whether Kelly Johnson receives advantages, such as access to the Capitol for her tours, that other nonprofits could not get. “Is it serving a political purpose or is it serving an actual charity?” said Philip Hackney, a professor at the University of Pittsburgh School of Law who specializes in nonprofit law. Without proper safeguards, young staffers could also feel pressured to participate in Johnson’s counseling and Bible study, said Davina Hurt, director of the government ethics program at Santa Clara University’s Markkula Center for Applied Ethics. She said it would be helpful to know who extends the invitations, whether the speaker’s name gets invoked and whether attendance is ever shared with the boss of a Hill staffer. “The institutional concern one should have is the power that’s present in those situations,” Hurt said. “If you want to advance through the ranks, you will feel pressure to some degree.” Haulsee said no staffers have ever been pressured to participate in Johnson’s programming. McGehee, the former ethics lobbyist, said she is sympathetic to the challenges a prominent politician’s spouse faces figuring out an appropriate role in Washington. But Onward Christian Education Services should at least articulate a firmer wall between Johnson and the money, she said, to avoid even the appearance of conflicts of interest. McGehee questioned why Johnson needed to be paid at all to minister to congressional staffers. “This is not about the value of the work,” McGehee said. “But it’s fraught.” In 2024, an IRS filing shows that Johnson took a salary of $50,000 even though the organization brought in no revenue that year, depleting its reserves to $5,797. Johnson said she was too busy with her husband’s new position to fundraise. The 2024 filing is the most recent financial statement available. item.title: House Democrats plan ambitious 100-day agenda if they sweep to power in midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — House Democrats are preparing an ambitious 100-days agenda focused on delivering their campaign promises — making life more affordable and conducting vast oversight of the Trump administration — if the party seizes majority control in next month's elections . Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries , who is in line to become House speaker if the party wins power, said the Democrats will be united “right out of the gate” on reinstating Affordable Care Act tax breaks , reversing Republican Medicaid cuts, holding votes against the Iran war and undoing President Donald Trump’s tariff regime . They expect to launch the agenda in the first 100 hours, once the new Congress is seated in January. “Fighting for an affordable America — that's what unites Democrats all across the country,” Jeffries said recently at the party campaign headquarters in Washington. “That’s our commitment to the American people, because the cost of living is way too high and far too many people who are working hard, playing by the rules, can’t thrive and can barely survive — and are drowning — in the Trump economy." It’s a hyper-focused agenda tapping into the voter sentiment that is driving much of the midterm election as Americans wrestle with affordability concerns and inflationary costs from the Iran war and other policies. The undertaking will also test the ability of the sprawling House Democrats to work together and avoid the chaotic divisions and disruptions that have hobbled Republicans under Speaker Mike Johnson’s leadership. Democrats have been out of power in the House since 2023. If Jeffries takes the helm, he would be the first Democratic speaker since Nancy Pelosi , leading a new generation of lawmakers that includes a handful of far-left candidates who are aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America . “The antidote to that is getting things done,” said Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski, who is poised to become chair of the New Democrat Coalition, the largest caucus within the House Democrats. She said the party is determined to show the American people that “Democrats know how to govern." A Freedom Caucus of the far-left? Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, the chairman of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, said he is often asked if Democrats will be confronting their own version of the Freedom Caucus, referring to the far-right Republicans who often grind the House agenda to a halt. “It doesn’t work that way," Casar told The Associated Press in an interview. “The Freedom Caucus breaks things. But if you're a progressive, you want to pass things.” Leader Jeffries, Casar and other Democrats have been in touch with the progressive candidates, many of whom are backed by the DSA as the party focuses on shared priorities. “This notion that because we'll have new members somehow we're going to be disjointed — not so,” said Louisiana Rep. Troy Carter, who hopes to become chair of the Congressional Black Caucus. "All those banking on that, save the popcorn for another day." The Republicans, who are confronting an increasingly difficult election-year climate to hold onto their majority, portray Democrats as beholden to a far-left socialist agenda. If Republicans retain power, Johnson has said they would press on with what they have already accomplished alongside Trump, which has been an agenda focused on cutting taxes and federal spending. “What we would do in the next two years is exactly what we have been doing already," Johnson said on CNBC's Squawk Box, “and that is putting the conditions in place for a strong America again.” Fix healthcare, stop the war, end the tariffs – and investigate Trump Months ago, Jeffries launched five working groups to tackle the affordability agenda focused on healthcare, housing, groceries and goods, gas and utilities, and care-giving. Each group is headed by a progressive and a centrist Democrat — the healthcare working group, for example, is run by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and Rep. Terri Sewell of Alabama — with the goal of striking common ground on draft policies that all House Democrats can support. At the same time, Jeffries has tasked the ranking Democrats on the House Oversight and Judiciary committees with preparing investigations. They are focused on Trump, his family and his administration, as part of a sweeping anti-corruption agenda. Impeachment , Jeffries has said, is neither on nor off the table. “We need to lower the cost of groceries and gas. Two, we need to make healthcare affordable for every single American. Three, we’re going to hold the crooks accountable who’ve visited unprecedented corruption on the American people,” Jeffries said. “Beginning on day one.” Democrats plan to vote quickly to reinstate the health care tax credits for the Affordable Care Act, which expired in 2025, leaving millions of Americans confronting higher health insurance costs. Proposals are also ready to reverse the Medicaid cuts that Republicans put in place as part of their “One Big Beautiful Bill” of tax breaks and program cuts, including new work requirements for recipients. There are measures to reverse Trump's tariffs as Congress works to claw back power from the White House. And Democrats, who have forced multiple votes on ending the Iran conflict, plan to pressure the Trump administration to end the military action by pushing forward more war powers resolutions. Much of the House Democrats' agenda, if they regain power, would depend on the size of the majority. Details also depend on the Senate, and whether it flips to Democrats. “We cannot simply go back to the status quo,” said Usamah Andrabi, a spokesman for Justice Democrats, an outside group that supports the far-left progressives. And Trump, at the White House, has ultimate say, with veto power at the stroke of a pen. “We’re going to do a lot and we’re going to be very busy,” Carter said. item.title: U.S. probe of Rep. Ilhan Omar reportedly focuses on birth date and citizenship papers
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The federal investigation that prompted the search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s D.C. residence on Monday centers on claims that she or her late father may have lied on decades-old immigration paperwork to secure legal status and eventually U.S. citizenship, three people familiar with the matter said. Omar - a Minnesota Democrat who was born in Somalia and fled civil war there with her family before eventually immigrating to the United States in 1995 - has repeatedly rejected such allegations, which have circulated in conservative media for years. She dismissed them again in a statement Monday as “baseless lies and smear campaigns.” Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. It is extremely unusual for federal agents to take public investigative actions related to a member of Congress just weeks before an election because doing so could cast a candidate who is not criminally charged in a negative light. In Omar’s case, the investigation is notable for other reasons as well: It involves long-ago paperwork from when she was a teenager, and Omar is a lawmaker who has frequently been singled out for criticism and vitriol by President Donald Trump and his allies. The president condemned her again in a social media post Tuesday, after U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro told Fox News that her office had launched a separate inquiry into Omar’s financial disclosure forms - a matter that has previously drawn the attention of House Republicans. “America wants answers, and we want them, NOW!” wrote Trump, mirroring his previous calls for Justice Department investigations of his perceived political enemies. The immigration-related inquiry, which could result in fraud charges and potentially an attempt by the Justice Department to strip Omar of her citizenship, is based on a renewed look at her immigration history launched earlier this year by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the investigative arm of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the people familiar with the matter said. The agency had declined to move forward with such a probe years earlier based on similar allegations, said one of the individuals, who is a former immigration official. That person and a Trump administration official said agents now are especially focused on whether Omar or her father, Nur Omar Mohamed, intentionally misstated her birth date on immigration paperwork so she could be eligible to derive citizenship through him as a minor when he was naturalized in 2000. Both of them, and a third person familiar with the investigation, spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss details that have not been made public. Investigators have also scrutinized whether Omar’s father may have purposefully lied or omitted information on his past military service as he sought legal status in the United States before he became a citizen, the Trump administration official said. Mohamed died in 2020. Both questions are considered key to the investigation because they led to Omar securing her citizenship. “HSI was just looking at her file top to bottom,” the official said. Some members of Omar’s family have received grand jury subpoenas tied to the investigation in recent days, according to another person familiar with the matter who also spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss investigative details. Omar, a frequent Trump critic and outspoken member of the Democratic progressive caucus, dismissed the probe in a statement Monday as the latest attempt by the Trump administration “to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” She declined an interview request Tuesday through her staff. The Department of Homeland Security and the White House referred requests for comment to the Justice Department. A spokesperson for Justice did not return requests for comment. Pirro’s separate investigation centers on paperwork Omar filed last year showing she and her husband held assets of between $6 and $30 million, a massive rise in wealth from her previous annual filing. Omar later revised that paperwork to declare assets between $18,000 to $95,000 and chalked up the earlier filing to an accounting error. A House watchdog recommended against misconduct findings against the congresswoman last month. Pirro’s acknowledgment to Fox that prosecutors were conducting their own investigation again appears at odds with long-standing Justice Department practice to avoid such statements about active candidates before elections. “It doesn’t matter what the House does,” she said. “We’re looking at the facts. Based on the facts, we’ll follow them wherever they take us.” The search warrant that Homeland Security agents served on Omar’s residence Monday listed potential charges of conspiracy, immigration fraud and false statements, one person familiar with document said. The Justice Department could opt to pursue charges along those lines or, if it believes it has proof that Omar’s improperly obtained her citizenship, it could pursue a criminal or civil denaturalization case against her. Criminal denaturalizations have a 10-year statute of limitations. Civil denaturalizations are not subject to a statute of limitations. The Justice Department under Trump has made denaturalization cases a priority, filing at least 163 since Trump took office in January 2025, federal officials said. Those include 40 cases since August, as the administration ramps up efforts to strip citizenship from people accused of concealing criminal histories and making false statements on their applications. But denaturalization cases have been historically rare, with an average of about 11 per year from 1990-2017, according to an analysis from the Migration Policy Institute. Such cases have rarely extended to decades-old actions except in cases tied to serious transnational crimes, including war crimes or genocide. Omar, in her memoir, has said that she and her family fled Somalia when she was around 8 as civil war engulfed the country. She spent four years in a Kenyan refugee camp and immigrated to the United States at age 12 in 1995. She gained citizenship as a minor through the naturalization of her father in 2000. The allegation that Omar was actually 18 at the time of her father’s citizenship application - and therefore ineligible to earn citizenship through her father - gained traction on conservative social media through a viral video posted in 2019. Shortly afterward, the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library, which maintains biographies of current and former state elected officials, revised Omar’s official birth year in its records from 1981 to 1982, a change that seemed to add momentum to the allegations. The library told The Washington Post on Tuesday that Omar’s staff had sought that change , saying at the time that it was in the process of correcting Omar’s birth year in various public sources. Omar, who served in the Minnesota House of Representatives from 2017 until joining Congress in 2019, also sought to change the birth year in Wikipedia and on the U.S. House of Representatives website, the library said. Omar has repeatedly characterized those requests as an attempt to correct mistakes, not to cover up the truth of her birth year. David Schmidtke, a reference librarian, told The Post the biographical information on its website is sometimes self-reported by legislators, their staff and family members. Immigration experts said it is not unusual for refugees, particularly from some African countries, to have issues providing accurate birth records. In Somalia, where Omar was born, only 6 percent of births were registered with the government, according to a 2020 Somali government report produced in collaboration with the United Nations. David Nakamura, Alexei Koseff and Razzan Nakhlawi contributed to this report. item.title: Bank of America hit with $1.2 billion penalty over money laundering failures
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Regulators fined Bank of America ( BAC ) more than $1.2 billion on Tuesday over widespread failures in the banking giant's safeguards against money laundering and other illicit financial activity. Bank of America stock fell 1% during premarket hours. The Treasury Department said the nation's second-largest bank failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions and to report more than $5 billion in suspicious activity, including transactions potentially tied to Chinese money-laundering networks, narcotics trafficking, and fraud. The enforcement actions include a $1.2 billion penalty from the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), the third-largest fine in the Treasury Department's history after it fined crypto exchange Binance $3.4 billion in 2023 and TD Bank for $1.3 billion in 2024. The fine also includes a $750 million penalty from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), the largest ever imposed by that regulator. The OCC penalty will be credited against FinCEN's assessment rather than added to it. Separately, a $11.6 million sanctions settlement brings the total penalties to more than $1.21 billion. "Even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. Bank of America's stock fell more than 2% after markets closed on Tuesday. It reports third quarter earnings Wednesday morning. The bank said it will include a "non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2 billion impacting net income by approximately 17 cents per share" in its third quarter results. "Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right," a Bank of America spokesperson said in an email statement, adding that the Charlotte, North Carolina based lender has invested "billions of dollars in technology" and dedicated "thousands of employees to combat financial crime" to resolve the deficiencies. Regulators said Bank of America's failures extended across its transaction monitoring systems, customer due diligence, and internal oversight. The bank failed to report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions, including over $1 billion involving national security-related and other priority illicit finance risks. FinCEN said Bank of America admitted to willfully violating the Bank Secrecy Act and had effectively outsourced substantial portions of its suspicious activity detection responsibilities to law enforcement and other financial institutions. The bank also prioritized revenue over compliance resources, according to Treasury, allowing suspicious transactions to go uninvestigated for extended periods. The penalties come nearly two years after Bank of America agreed to a December 2024 cease-and-desist order requiring it to address longstanding weaknesses in its anti-money laundering controls. The OCC said the bank failed to make sufficient progress despite that earlier enforcement action. "Bank of America's poor response to its [Bank Secrecy Act] deficiencies is unacceptable," Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould said, describing continued breakdowns in internal controls. Separately, Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control announced an $11.6 million settlement involving 475 apparent violations of sanctions programs targeting Russia, Iran, and other countries and activities. As part of the latest enforcement actions, Bank of America must conduct a review of previously undetected suspicious transactions with an outside party and undergo independent assessments of its compliance controls. Mike Mayo, a Wells Fargo equity analyst who covers the bank called the action a "black eye" for Bank of America while describing the one-time charge as "digestible." item.title: Justice Department threatens California over alleged noncitizen voters, letter shows
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Jacob Bogage and Andrew Goudsward WASHINGTON, Oct 13 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department on Tuesday gave California officials 48 hours to review a list of alleged noncitizen voters or face legal action, according to a letter reviewed by Reuters - part of an unprecedented effort to find evidence ‌of voter fraud ahead of next month's elections. The letter, written by acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter and addressed to California Secretary ‌of State Shirley Weber, says the Justice Department provided officials in Los Angeles County with a "password-protected thumb drive" with the names of people the federal government "believes are likely noncitizens" and were sent mail-in ballots. The ​letter demands that the state refuse to send ballots to those on the list until their citizenship status has been confirmed. Voters in question who have already received ballots should have their ballot "segregated" once it is mailed back; ballots already returned should not be tabulated "until citizenship has been determined," the letter stipulates. The federal government "will have no choice but to seek emergency relief," according to the letter, if state officials do not follow its instructions. "Allowing noncitizens to vote cancels citizen votes," McCotter wrote. The letter marks an escalation of the ‌Trump administration's attempts to pressure states over alleged voting ⁠by non-US citizens and signals the Justice Department may be prepared to challenge ballots in the weeks leading up to the November 3 election, when Republicans will be defending their narrow majorities in Congress. Justice Department spokeswoman Kiersten Pels confirmed the existence of the ⁠letter in a statement to Reuters, adding: "The department will take all necessary legal action to protect election integrity and ensure compliance with federal law.” Representatives from the White House and the California secretary of state's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment. FRAUD CLAIMS The Justice Department under President Donald Trump has repeatedly claimed that voting by non-US citizens is widespread, ​despite ​multiple studies showing it is rare. Though states may have added more than 30,000 noncitizens to ​their voter rolls since 2000 due to software glitches and clerical ‌errors, Reuters found in September, it was unclear how many had cast a ballot. Experts said the numbers were too small relative to the country’s 170 million registered voters to affect elections. In July, the Justice Department sent letters to chief election officials in all 50 states warning they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls or cast ballots. The department's Civil Rights Division has demanded nonpublic voter data, including voters' Social Security numbers or dates of birth, from nearly all states as part of its hunt for noncitizens on state rolls. It has sued 30 Democratic- and Republican-led states that refused to hand over their ‌rolls, but has lost 26 of those cases without winning one. Reuters reported last month that the ​Department of Homeland Security was using a commercial data broker to find sensitive voter information not included ​in publicly available rolls, which officials and experts warned could lead to ​citizens being falsely flagged as illegal voters and potentially detained. Federal prosecutors have also ramped up prosecutions of noncitizens for allegedly voting ‌in past elections or submitting fraudulent registrations, touting 16 new criminal ​cases on Monday. Officials in Democratic-led California have tussled ​for months with the Trump administration over its attempts to intervene in election procedures over allegations of voter fraud. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin informed California officials on July 16 that the federal government believed the state had noncitizens on its voting rolls, according to the letter. California could prove pivotal in deciding ​control of the US House of Representatives, especially after ‌the state's voters approved a new congressional map that heavily favors Democrats as part of a nationwide redistricting sprint that began in Republican-led ​states. Voters in Los Angeles will also weigh in on a ballot measure that would allow certain noncitizen legal residents to cast ballots in municipal elections. (Reporting by ​Jacob Bogage and Andrew Goudsward in Washington; Editing by Jesse Mesner-Hage and Jamie Freed) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/exclusive-us-justice-department-threatens-034849746.html

item.title: Iran ramps up attacks on ships in bid to keep oil prices high before U.S. midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Parisa Hafezi, Jonathan Saul and Phil Stewart DUBAI/LONDON/WASHINGTON, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Iran is deploying new tactics to target ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz as it seeks to keep oil prices high and influence the US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters. Tehran has tried to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz since the US and Israel ‌launched strikes against Iran on February 28. It has restricted passage through the waterway, which carried about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade before the war, in an effort ‌to gain leverage over Washington. Its threats and attacks have severely curtailed traffic through the strait, driving up oil prices, though some oil has continued to transit. The two officials declined to provide details of the new strategy, but one said that Iran had started using ​different offensive tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions about 10 days ago, adding that this had led to an increase in attacks on such ships. The strategy included a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the US vote, they said. "The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices," one of the two officials said. The decision to adopt the new strategy had been taken at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership and was fully coordinated across the country’s ruling system, the officials said. IRAN USING SPOTTERS A US military official, speaking on condition ‌of anonymity, confirmed that Iran had changed tactics in one significant way: ⁠after the US destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had started using unarmed spotters in small boats to identify potential targets, including US naval vessels, the official said. Last week, in a previously unreported incident, the US military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from a dhow, calling in targets to the IRGC, ⁠the official said. US forces confronted the vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it. There were no casualties, the US official said. Unwilling to risk its remaining fast boats, Iran had been unable to prevent a ramp-up in oil exports through the strait, the official said, particularly after US strikes devastated its navy. The war — and its $3 billion monthly price tag — has become a key issue on the US campaign trail for November's midterm elections, which will decide control ​of ​Congress. US President Donald Trump has been weighing next steps against Iran, but has said he will not attack again before the ​vote. The US has meanwhile been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports and ‌extending sanctions as it tries to pile economic pressure on Tehran to reach a deal to end the conflict. The standoff over Hormuz has left global energy markets exposed to further disruption, with the threat of attacks and high shipping and insurance costs complicating efforts to restore normal traffic. In recent days, attacks on commercial ships still sailing through the strait have surged to their highest level since the war began, according to independent data. There have been at least five incidents in the past 48 hours involving tankers and other commercial ships around the Hormuz area, including drone strikes, according to data analysis from maritime security sources and incidents reported to British navy-affiliated agency United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO). That approximately mirrored the rate of attacks on October 3-5, pointing to a new escalation, according to data from the UN shipping agency, the International Maritime Organization. "There is a tempo increase ‌in strikes, which looks deliberate," one maritime security source said. ATTACKS OVER AN EXPANDED AREA As part of the new strategy, Tehran will ​also expand the geographical scope of its operations beyond the Strait of Hormuz to the Gulf of Oman and waters further afield, ​the officials said. Analysis by maritime security sources based on attacks reported to UKMTO and maritime security ​companies in the region suggest this may already be happening. They show Iran targeting ships in areas beyond the Strait of Hormuz, including waters off the coast of Qatar ‌and the United Arab Emirates, in recent days. The second Iranian official added that ​Tehran would not allow Trump to bring down oil prices ​before the November elections. "Just when they think they are getting close to the point where prices will fall, we will push them away from it. This is a game of chess,” the second official said. "Such vessels would be safe nowhere, even outside the Strait of Hormuz." The Pentagon and Iran's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment. COMPLETE CLOSURE OF HORMUZ SOON, SAYS IRANIAN OFFICIAL Both ​Iranian officials said Tehran is moving towards a situation in which no vessel ‌violating its restrictions would be able to pass through the strait. "It will be complete closure soon," one of the officials said. In its latest report on Sunday, the US Navy-led Joint Maritime ​Information Center (JMIC) said the threat to merchant shipping in the Strait of Hormuz remained "severe", the second-highest level. "IRGC attacks, attempted attacks, and/or harassment activity persisted including UAV overflight, targeted surveillance of merchant shipping, ​and occasional VHF hailing," JMIC said. (Reporting by Parisa Hafezi, Jonathan Saul and Phil Stewart; Editing by Aidan Lewis) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/iran-shifting-tactics-step-attacks-000632093.html

item.title: 'The baby boomers have arrived': Americans over 75 got richer than other age groups
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
For millions of families in the US, wealth has inched up modestly in the last few years, but for older Americans, it's surged. People 75 and older are now the richest group in the US, according to the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances. The survey, published every three years, found that the median family net worth in the US, adjusted for inflation, rose 2% to $215,900 between 2022 and 2025. But among the 75 and older cohort, their median net worth rose 37% to $505,000, compared with $367,000 in 2022. Families younger than 35, meanwhile, saw their median net worth dive 23% to $33,000. As Mark Zandi, Moody's chief economist, told Yahoo Finance: "The baby boomers have arrived!" "The oldest of the large boomer generation has aged into the 75 and older age group, and the surging stock market has benefited older Americans more because they have more of their wealth in retirement accounts," he said. Wealth inequality on display This isn't startling news given long-held patterns of wealth inequality in America. "On balance, wealth inequality appears little changed since 2022," according to the Fed research. "These changes in wealth largely reinforced existing patterns of wealth inequality by family characteristics." Groups that typically have less wealth — young people, renters, and those without a high school diploma — saw their wealth slip in the years following the pandemic. Families that already had more wealth, whether thanks to age or higher income, saw some of the largest gains. One reason: Higher-income families tend to save more, which in turn helps their wealth grow even more. "Net worth tends to increase and then plateau (or decline) over the life cycle, reflecting changes in savings behavior that occur with age as individuals save for retirement throughout their working career and then spend those savings in retirement," per the report. Importantly, a variety of other factors, aside from age, come into play, including education, race, and whether you've built up equity in a home. For example, when the head of a family had a college degree, they had 1.9 times the median income of those with some college and almost 3 times the median net worth. Stocks and home values lift Americans' net worth It makes sense that many older baby boomers who bought homes and stocks decades ago have seen their assets take off in value. Between the start of 2022 and the end of 2025, the S&P 500 gained roughly 52.41% on a total return basis (including reinvested dividends). For families owning a home, the median net housing value (home value minus debt) rose from $218,900 in 2022 to $230,000 in 2025, according to the Federal Reserve report. Many of those 75 and older may have bought homes when prices were a whisper of what they are today. A typical three-bedroom home in northwest Washington, D.C., for example, purchased three decades ago for under $300,000 could easily have been valued at roughly $1 million in 2025, according to Zillow. "Higher interest rates also helped as this group has a lot of wealth tied up in CDs and other interest-bearing assets," Zandi added. The Social Security factor Social Security is a key factor in older Americans' wealth gains, said Laurence Kotlikoff, a Boston University economics professor and Social Security expert. "Social Security benefits have risen substantially more rapidly than median wages, and that has been happening for some time. People 75-plus who've been able to get Social Security for probably now 13 years, or at least 10 years, have benefited from that as opposed to those who are in the younger age group and on the job," he said. From December 2015 to December 2025, median weekly wages outpaced inflation, according to Pew Research Center data. But over the five years leading up to December 2025, real wages fell after factoring in inflation. Social Security benefits, on the other hand, have increased by a cumulative total of approximately 35.5% over the past 10 years through annual Cost of Living Adjustments (COLA), according to the Social Security Administration. On the flip side: Rising senior poverty While many boomers are truly living their golden years, more seniors are spending them in poverty . Poverty among Americans age 65 and older rose for the fifth consecutive year and has jumped roughly 45% since 2019 — the highest rate of any age group, a recent AARP Foundation analysis of Census data found. That translates to 10 million seniors living in poverty, up from 5.1 million seven years ago. "No other age group has seen that same pattern, and that should really stop us in our tracks. It's alarming," said AARP Foundation president Claire Casey. The poverty slide starts well before age 65. More than 7 million people in their 50s and early 60s are already living in poverty, Casey said. The barriers to saving: healthcare costs, inflation, long-term care, wages failing to keep pace with expenses, and debt. Kerry Hannon is a Senior Columnist at Yahoo Finance. item.title: New inflation data comes in hotter than expected as prices remain high ahead of midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Inflation heated up to 3.7% annually last month as energy prices soared, according to the latest Consumer Price Index data. The latest reading came in hot, accelerating from 3.4% in August and outpacing economists' expected 3.6% jump. On a monthly basis, prices rose 0.6% in September from 0.4% a month earlier. Gas prices were a particularly large driver of the jump, rising 9.1% month over month. Average prices at the pump hit a record $4.33 last month , according to AAA data, nearly $0.50 above the previous monthly record set in 2023. Fuel oil, which millions of Americans, primarily in the Northeast, use to heat their homes, was another pain point , spiraling 15.3% from August just before the cold months set in. "Core" inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices and is watched more closely by Federal Reserve officials , was also hotter than expected, rising 2.6% annually, up from 2.4% in August. Monthly core inflation was unchanged from August's hotter-than-anticipated 0.3% but also came in higher than the 0.2% economists were expecting. "Some CPI reports seem backward looking and stale, while others seem like they're foreshadowing what's to come. This one definitely feels like the latter," Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com, said in a statement. He called the uptick in core inflation "worrying." On a core basis, the cost of travel and leisure was a major driver of inflation. Car rental costs rose 5.4% from a month earlier, while hotels were up 2.3%. Football and soccer fans are also paying up, with the average cost of a sporting event ticket up 7.6%. "This makes the October meeting live," Stephanie Roth, Wolfe Research chief economist, told Yahoo Finance. Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, said in a statement that the latest report might not be hot enough to justify a hike this month, but inflation clearly remains a problem. item.title: Pope Leo spends peaceful night in hospital after surgery for lung cancer
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Joshua McElwee VATICAN CITY, Oct 14 (Reuters) - World leaders, Catholics across the globe and senior cardinals at the Vatican offered prayers for Pope Leo on Wednesday after doctors announced the 71-year-old pontiff had been diagnosed with lung cancer and had part of one ‌lung removed. The cancer diagnosis for a pope known to be relatively young and energetic and who was elected only in May 2025 ‌caused shock. A prayer was recited for Leo to have a good convalescence and complete healing during an open-air Mass in St. Peter's Square on Wednesday following the surgery. The pope was diagnosed on ​Tuesday with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer, after doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung during an operation. Leo spent a peaceful night in hospital, the Vatican said, adding that further information about his condition would be released later on Wednesday. The pontiff had been admitted to Rome's Gemelli hospital after doctors discovered a growth during a recent routine health check. The operation lasted about 90 minutes and was completed without complications, the pope's lead surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, ‌and his personal physician, Luigi Carbone, said late on ⁠Tuesday. The doctors said in a joint statement that the entire lower lobe of the right lung was removed in an effort to eliminate all cancerous tissue. Human lungs have five lobes — three in the right lung and two in the ⁠left. The Vatican has not disclosed the size of the tumour or whether the disease had spread to nearby lymph nodes, key factors in determining prognosis. Leo is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to have had recent health issues. BEST WISHES AND PRAYERS The Vatican said ​earlier ​this week that the pope was expected to remain in hospital for about a ​week and that all his public engagements had been cancelled until ‌October 20. The Mass on Wednesday was the closing act of an assembly of bishops called by Leo to discuss the Church's family life teachings, the largest gathering of Church leaders so far during this papacy. Filipino Cardinal Luis Tagle led the Mass in place of Leo. The pope last week approved Tagle as the dean of the Church's College of Cardinals, in the first selection of an Asian cleric to the elite role. Political leaders offered messages of support. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he and his wife Jeanette were praying for the pope, an American who was born in Chicago. "May the Lord give him strength ‌and the Holy Spirit guide the medical professionals taking care of the Holy Father," ​he said on X. Rubio met Leo at the Vatican in May. There was no immediate response ​on social media from US President Donald Trump, who has criticised ​the pope, or his Vice President JD Vance, who is a Catholic. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen sent her ‌best wishes. "His serenity and strength are an inspiration for all ​of us. We hope for his full ​and speedy recovery," she wrote on X. SOUTH AMERICAN TRIP SCHEDULED Leo normally follows a very busy schedule. He is due to make a tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, but it was not clear if this trip would still go ahead. The pope is ​the ultimate earthly authority for the world's 1.4 billion ‌Catholics and does not have a deputy who steps in when he is sick. When a pope is incapacitated, the business of ​the Vatican's vast bureaucracy carries on as usual, holding off on any decisions that require papal approval. item.title: World's oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkey — and some of its cargo has survived
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The world's oldest shipwreck has been discovered off the coast of Turkey, archaeologists say. They have dated it to between 4,400 and 4,700 years old, which is the Early Bronze Age, and is around the same time that the Great Pyramid was being built. The ship's wooden structure has not survived, but the ceramic storage pots it was carrying were lying on the sea floor and, remarkably, some still contain traces of what they held inside. The archaeologists who found the ship say it was about 10m in length and was a trade vessel carrying cargo across the Mediterranean Sea. "The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea," said Prof Hakan Öniz, from Akdeniz University in Turkey, who led the Mediterranean Archaeology Association expedition. The divers found three stone anchors, as ships carried spares on long voyages [Hakan Öniz] The wreck is close to the shore of Kekova Island in Antalya, Turkey. The artefacts lie scattered across an underwater slope, just 30m beneath the waves. Three large stone anchors were found, as well as more than 30 ceramic storage pots, called amphorae. The fact that none of the ship's wood remained meant techniques like radiocarbon dating - which measures a form of carbon in organic materials - could not be used to determine its age. Instead, archaeologists analysed the shape of the amphorae. Because pottery styles have changed over time, different styles are linked to particular periods. The Kekova ceramics are distinctive, with two handles, a ridge in the middle and a flat base. Öniz said this design matched other amphorae unearthed in Egypt and the Middle East that were known to be 4,400-4,700 years old. "Comparing the decoration techniques… we can definitely say our wreck is Early Bronze Age. This is 100%." The amphorae were recovered and taken on board the research ship [Hakan Öniz] After thousands of years underwater, the fragile artefacts are now being carefully conserved [Hakan Öniz] Divers from the expedition brought the pots up to the surface, where they are now being carefully conserved after so many thousands of years underwater. Dr Karin Sowada, an archaeologist from Macquarie University, Australia, examined the amphorae after they were recovered. Some were intact and she was surprised to see they still contained a viscous, glossy residue. "I looked inside and nearly fainted. I could not believe how much [residue] was visible. It wasn't just like spots…. a lot of this material was still remaining," she said. The team is now working to find out exactly what was being carried in the amphorae. "It could be olive oil, it could be wine, it could be tree resins," Sowada said. "It's possible that [the residue] could actually be the result of reuse of the jars. I mean, these jars are huge - they're not things that you just ship away and then never see again. People would have emptied these jars on arrival and potentially used them for many, many, many years." [BBC] The wreck and its cargo are also shedding light on trade in the ancient world. The archaeologists say the ship started its voyage from somewhere along the eastern coast of the Mediterranean. They believe it was taking goods to either the ancient city of Troy, in what is now north-western Turkey, or to the Minoan people in Crete. The divers worked underwater to carefully excavate the artefacts [Hakan Öniz] Travelling by sea was fraught with danger, particularly around Kekova Island, where the strong currents and winds have claimed many ships. There are hundreds of wrecks in the area, and the Mediterranean Archaeology Association specialises in finding and studying them. Öniz says that when he is diving on the wreck his first thoughts are about the lives of the people who were connected to this vessel. "We are the first humans who [have] touched these objects after 5,000 years. "We are always thinking of the sailors... the producers of the amphora and the person who carried the amphora on their shoulders to the ship, and the women who were waiting for their husbands, and they unfortunately couldn't go back." The shipwreck is owned by the Turkish Ministry of Culture. Its minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said the artefacts that have been recovered would be put on display in the new Mediterranean Underwater Archaeology Museum in Antalya when it opens in the coming months. The depth meant the divers could only spend 30 minutes at a time exploring it [Hakan Öniz] The Kekova discovery now tops the list of the world's oldest shipwrecks. Previously, the record holder was a wreck off the coast of Dokos, an island in southern Greece, which dates to about 4,200 years ago. The oldest known intact shipwreck, where the wood is still preserved, was found in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria. It dates to about 2,400 years ago. item.title: House control all but gone, top Republicans privately concede
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Some top congressional Republicans have privately concluded that it is likely impossible for them to keep control of the House of Representatives in the midterm elections, and they are now focused on limiting the scale of the defeat and salvaging the party's Senate majority. Five senior Republican lawmakers, all granted anonymity to speak candidly about their party's dire position, told POLITICO the House had all but slipped away. One senior House Republican said the GOP's goal at this point was to "save as many Republican seats as we can." The president, this person said, was not helping. "President Trump has made this election all about himself," the lawmaker said. "Now we have to survive that political storm." A second Republican member of Congress said the movement of campaign advertising made plain which side was in control of the midterms. This lawmaker predicted Democrats would pick up about 10 seats, more than enough to take control of the chamber. Even in newly redistricted red states like Florida and Texas, this person said, Republican candidates were "hanging on with their fingernails." Republicans have already fallen back from several contested House districts that they feel are no longer winnable, including those held by Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa and Tom Kean Jr. of New Jersey. Trump carried their districts just two years ago. The party last week gave up on an Omaha-based district held by retiring Rep. Don Bacon. Trump officials and other top GOP operatives say more candidates may be cut off in the coming days, in order to shift advertising money to races where it can make more of a difference. Republican groups have already given up on multiple races where they once hoped to unseat Democratic lawmakers. The Republican Party is under extreme pressure across the Midwest, where it is now spending heavily to defend Senate seats in once-reliably MAGA states like Iowa, Nebraska and Kansas. Bacon, a maverick often at odds with the White House, said there was no mystery in his party's political tribulations. "I've talked to some who are making these decisions: The biggest problem is the president's polling numbers and unfavorables," Bacon said. White House officials insist they're not giving up on either chamber of Congress. In a statement, White House spokeswoman Liz Huston said Trump remained "committed to maintaining Republican majorities in both the House and Senate." As he departed on Tuesday to campaign in Alaska for embattled GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan, Trump professed optimism about the midterms but acknowledged that sitting presidents typically see their party lose seats in the off year. "But I'm doing a tour right now and I'm doing rallies," Trump added. "The level of enthusiasm for the Republican Party is way up." House Speaker Mike Johnson went even further, flatly declaring during a campaign stop in deep-red Texas that "the polling is wrong" in showing his party on the brink of a broad defeat. Yet at a tactical level, the Republican Party's moves to shift money away from defending the House and toward saving the Senate are clear enough. In recent days, the Congressional Leadership Fund, the top super PAC for House Republicans, canceled advertising for key House candidates in Nebraska and Iowa and allowed the Senate Leadership Fund – a Republican group focused on the upper chamber – to swoop in and claim the airtime to support Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts and Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is running for Senate in Iowa. "These are not the moves of a party that's going to keep the House," a third Republican lawmaker said. In statements to POLITICO, both CLF and the National Republican Congressional Committee said they had no intention of giving up on the fight for control of the House. NRCC spokesperson Mike Marinella said districts are won "one by one," and that the GOP has "the financial firepower and ground game needed to win." Chris Winkelman, president of CLF, said his group would keep moving money around to maximize the impact nationally. The goal, he said, was to "keep the pressure on the most vulnerable Democrats and preserve a path to 218 seats." Former Rep. Carlos Curbelo, a Florida Republican who lost his swing seat in Trump's first midterm election eight years ago, said his former colleagues were clear-eyed about where the election seemed to be headed. "The environment is about as tough as one could expect," Curbelo said. "There is no one who has privately stated that they believe Republicans can hold the House — not in recent weeks, anyway." Megan Messerly, Lauren Fedor, Lisa Kashinsky and Myah Ward contributed to this report.
