item.title: White House officials question how long Katie Zacharia can last after 1st press briefing
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Several White House officials are questioning how long Katie Zacharia will keep the press secretary job after her first briefing Tuesday, saying her performance was unlikely to satisfy President Donald Trump. Several advisers and officials offered negative reviews of the briefing to CNN, with one characterizing it as "brutal." Others described it as unusual, awkward, stilted and, at times, uncomfortable. Zacharia appeared at the podium for only about 15 minutes, and most of that time was dedicated to an opening statement touting Trump's accomplishments. She called on only three reporters for questions before ending the briefing. Some White House officials and Trump advisers expressed confusion about why the White House rushed Zacharia to the podium. A source familiar with the matter said Trump had asked Zacharia to conduct the briefing, and while some in his orbit had misgivings, the source was unaware of anyone relaying them to Zacharia or Trump. "She should have been doing murder boards for two weeks before going up there," one Trump adviser told CNN, before critiquing Zacharia's performance. "The best thing she did was break the news about [Ambassador to Greece Kimberly] Guilfoyle — at least that takes the focus off of her performance." "Why did they put her out there so quickly?" a White House official said incredulously. "Literally zero reason to put her out on her second day, unprepared." Trump praised Zacharia after the briefing, telling reporters shortly after: "I thought she was very good." White House communications director Steven Cheung also said in a statement to CNN that "Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team." Zacharia planned ahead of time that she would give lengthy introductory remarks, based on what Trump had requested, and take only take three questions – from outlets she chose ahead of time, a source familiar with the matter said. The briefing was notably shorter than what had become the norm. Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt's briefings lasted for about an average of 45 minutes. During her first briefing, she called on two "new media" reporters before an Associated Press correspondent. She would also take questions from reporters standing in the aisles. Zacharia called on reporters from conservative outlet Breitbart, which was in the "new media" seat, Fox News and the Daily Mail. She appeared to have their names written down ahead of time. Trump and Zacharia met briefly ahead of the briefing, and Trump told her he was seeking Guilfoyle's resignation, a source said. unknown content item - Another adviser told CNN that while Zacharia "wasn't great," it was just her first press briefing. They expected Trump would give her the benefit of the doubt. Trump had grown somewhat infatuated with Zacharia's appearances on Fox News before eventually hiring her, sources told CNN. But one of the advisers noted that appearing on a cable TV panel and standing in front of the world at the podium were two different things. "No question we're all missing Karoline," said one adviser. Zacharia said she was cutting the briefing short because Trump would likely soon take reporter questions on the White House South Lawn before he departed for Alaska. "I am going to end it because President Trump is heading out to Marine One for our historic trip to Alaska, and we can ask him all of the questions out there," she said. Questions have also surfaced online about Zacharia's status as an attorney , and CNN has found no evidence that she has passed the bar exam in the states where she has lived and worked since graduating Pepperdine Caruso School of Law. When Trump announced her new role, he referred to his new press secretary as "an attorney." "The State Bar of California has no record of Kate Sharon Zacharia or Kate Sharon Black having been licensed to practice law in California," a spokesperson for the California State Bar told CNN in a statement, referring to her maiden name. "Due to confidentiality requirements, the State Bar can only confirm whether someone passed the bar exam, not whether they took the bar exam." When a reporter pressed Trump at the White House on Tuesday morning about what state Zacharia passed the bar exam in, the president turned to his new press secretary, who was standing behind him. "Which state?" Trump asked Zacharia. She responded that she had moved to China. In response to questions on her legal credentials, a White House official told CNN that Zacharia moved to China with her husband after graduating law school, citing his job at an American private equity firm, and that she worked on international transaction law at the time. The official did not respond to a follow-up question about whether she passed the bar exam. According to her LinkedIn profile, Zacharia worked as an associate on the international practice team at Zhong Lun Law in Beijing from August 2011 to June 2013. She was also general counsel to Fix California , an elections-focused nonprofit founded by Trump ally Ric Grenell, from January 2024 to March 2025. Her most recent position was senior communications adviser for the Trump Media and Technology Group. It is unclear on what cadence Zacharia will brief reporters. A CNN Reliable Sources analysis of the White House video archive found Leavitt, who departed the role in August, held formal briefings about once a week on average before having her second child. She held 14 briefings in the four months leading up to her maternity leave in late April. She held another 49 briefings through the rest of 2025, which included several nontraditional briefings. item.title: Texas DA says ICE officer intentionally ran over immigrant and may face charges
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
HOUSTON — Videos collected by local investigators make it “pretty obvious” that an ICE officer intentionally ran over Miguel Parra Hernandez during an immigration stop Saturday, which could lead to assault charges, the district attorney said Tuesday. “This was an intentional striking and running over of the person by the vehicle, and in that case, that is an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in Texas,” Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare told NBC News. Teare said the federal government is not cooperating with the investigation conducted by his office and the Harris County Sheriff’s Office. He also said ICE may have allowed the erasure of critical data in the vehicle involved in striking Parra, who was on foot. Teare said that in his seven years as a Harris County vehicular crimes division chief, he has reviewed video from a number of other auto-pedestrian collision cases. He said the video his investigators have gathered in Parra’s case “goes above” the video that was posted online and obtained by NBC affiliate KPRC of Houston. “My viewing of it, and many other investigators that have viewed it, as well, it’s pretty obvious that this was an intentional striking and running over of the person by the vehicle, and in that case, that is an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in Texas,” he said. Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare. (Raquel Natalicchio / Houston Chronicle via Getty) Parra, 48, was left with multiple breaks and fractures in his body, according to his attorney and an advocate who has been speaking on his behalf. He had surgery on one leg and faces multiple additional operations, said Cesar Espinosa, co-founder and executive director of FIEL, an immigrant civil rights group. Video obtained by KPRC shows a white truck headed in the opposite direction of traffic on a busy roadway. It shows a vehicle jumping a yellow median and heading in the direction that Parra is running. It then appears to show the vehicle, which is not marked, swerving left toward Parra’s path, in front of a truck stopped in a shopping center. The parked truck leaves, and a man can be seen on the pavement behind the ICE vehicle, the video shows. An ICE spokesman said over the weekend that officers were pursuing the fleeing men and that “Miguel Parra Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck.” Teare, a Democrat, announced late Monday that his office had launched an independent investigation. On Tuesday, an ICE spokesperson who was not identified said in a statement that “allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE. The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct.” ICE said the allegations are “disgusting smears” that are “peddled by the media,” leading to more than a 1,600% increase in assaults and a 3,300% increase in vehicle attacks against its law enforcement officers. It did not offer data behind those numbers. ICE has said that Parra was not the target of the attempted stop but that he was in the country illegally. Parra’s attorney and family have said he has no criminal record and was on his way to work applying stucco. Teare said his office and the sheriff’s office determined that the vehicle that struck Parra was a Jeep Cherokee and that it potentially had evidence, including a data crash recorder. He said his office wanted to know whether the vehicle locked in information at the time of the collision that could be downloaded, such as speed, steering and braking. Teare said the way to preserve data from the car would have been to “put it on a flatbed trailer and you take it to forensically download it.” But he said he believes any data on the recorder related to the incident could have been erased when ICE drove the car away. He and the sheriff’s investigators told ICE the information needed to be downloaded, but ICE refused, Teare said. ICE did not respond to questions about a data crash recorder, the erasing of any potential data or any refusal to download it. “Our office began drafting a search warrant that we were in the process of drafting when the ICE agent in question, the one that had been driving, we believed, at the time of the collision, jumped back into the car and drove it away from the scene,” Teare said. “In my 20-year career, I’ve never heard of anything like that.” Teare also said two people from “an entirely different operation” were in the back seat of the ICE vehicle when it struck Parra. Those two people are also in ICE custody, along with Parra. Teare said his office is working to ensure all three remain in the country as material witnesses. “I’ve taught for years at the Houston Police Department Academy, Harris County Department Academy. I’ve worked with law enforcement for 20 years. There is not a single agency in the United States that would teach that once you put people in custody in your car, you then begin to pursue other people,” he said. Doing so puts “every single person out there in danger again,” he said. According to Teare, the ICE vehicle should have activated its emergency equipment, such as its lights and siren, as it jumped a median and crossed into oncoming traffic. A senior official at the Department of Homeland Security told NBC News on Tuesday that multiple ICE officers on the scene at the time were wearing body cameras. ICE is reviewing video of the scene as part of an internal investigation, the official said. Espinosa said Parra told him that he fled because it was unclear whether there were officials in the vehicles, which he said were unmarked, did not use sirens and had dark, tinted windows. ICE has said it was targeting another man, Jose Mendoza Cervantes, who was in the country illegally and had committed several crimes. Espinoza and Parra’s attorney Kim Bruno said neither Parra nor the man who was with him when ICE stopped their vehicle has any association with Mendoza. Miguel Parra Hernandez. (Noticias Telemundo) In previous encounters between ICE and targets of its arrests in vehicle stops, including some who have been killed, such as Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston , ICE has alleged the people it tried to arrest weaponized their vehicles . Parra was struck less than two weeks after the Trump administration issued guidance setting tighter rules for vehicle stops. The guidance says only agents who have completed specific training should make vehicle stops. The memo also says that vehicles used for traffic stops must have lights and sirens and that all officers on the scenes of vehicle stops must wear and activate their body cameras. The Harris County District Attorney’s Office has been asking witnesses and people who may have photos or video of the incident to contact it. Teare said that there is a secure portal that goes directly to the district attorney’s office and that no one is asked about citizenship or immigration status. “All we are interested in is getting the truth, and any shred of cellphone footage, anyone that saw something and really can point us in the right direction, it would be wonderful,” he said. item.title: Mamdani and city council speaker strike deal to ban NYC horse carriage industry
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
NEW YORK — Mayor Zohran Mamdani and New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin have reached a deal to abolish the city's horse carriage industry — a critical breakthrough in a decadeslong, politically fraught effort to ban the tourist attraction. Since 2010, mayors and local legislative leaders have tried to outlaw horse-drawn carriages from operating in Central Park, citing concerns about the safety of the animals as several have died in accidents and from exhaustion. But despite broad popular support, the efforts have failed, in large part due to political pressure from New York's powerful transport union, which advocates for hundreds of carriage drivers who make a living shuttling tourists on buggies around the park. Now, that stalemate appears closer than ever to being broken. In an announcement shared exclusively with POLITICO on Tuesday, a Menin spokesperson said Mamdani's administration has agreed to back a bill that would make it illegal to operate a horse-drawn carriage in the city, starting in June 2028. With Mamdani onboard, Menin — who first announced her support for the bill in July — said she's scheduling a full Council vote on the measure for Oct. 22. The legislation has already secured formal support from more than half of the Council's 51 members, meaning it's on a glidepath to becoming law now that Mamdani is committed to supporting it. "Horse-drawn carriages have long been part of New York City's history, but in an increasingly busy Central Park, this tradition has become a growing public safety liability," Menin said in a statement. "Next week, the Council will take decisive action by voting on [this bill] to protect New Yorkers, visitors, and the horses themselves." Mamdani spokesperson Sneha Choudhary confirmed the mayor and the speaker have reached a deal on the legislation. She also said Mamdani is committed to working on helping carriage drivers find new work and added: "We have been working closely with the City Council, union partners, carriage drivers, animal welfare advocates, and community leaders to deliver a just transition that protects workers while ending horse-drawn carriages in Central Park once and for all." Mamdani and Menin will, no doubt, be hailed by animal rights activists, who have long fought to ban the horse carriage industry, arguing it puts both animals and humans in danger. On the flipside, the announcement isn't without political risk, especially for Mamdani, who has courted support from the Transport Workers Union, which advocates for horse carriage drivers and has been aggressively opposed to any plan that would disband the industry outright. The TWU has pushed for an alternative bill in the Council that would leave the industry in place with new safety regulations. In response to news of the deal, Transport Workers Union International President John Samuelsen, whose New York members are mostly subway, bus and railway workers, blasted the finalized version of the bill for giving "no meaningful economic relief for workers." "This is disgraceful political opportunism, and Zohran should not simply go along with it, particularly when immigrant families' livelihoods are being destroyed," Samuelsen said. "This entire situation is reprehensible." Mamdani has long said he supports the concept of outlawing the horse carriage industry, but prior to Monday, he had withheld support for the Council bill under consideration, arguing it did not go far enough in ensuring protections for the horse carriage drivers who'd lose their livelihoods. Ultimately, Mamdani — a democratic socialist who has positioned himself as a friend of organized labor — came around to backing the bill because the latest version includes several new labor safeguards, according to the speaker's office. Under the updated bill, which was shared with POLITICO, the city must create a workforce transition program under which carriage drivers would receive career counseling as well as referrals to employment opportunities in both public and private sectors, including with the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, local sight-seeing bus companies and pedicab operators. Additionally, the bill requires the city to "consider" establishing programs to compensate carriage owners for the value of their businesses, their horses, their equipment and the licenses they hold to operate. The bill, which was first introduced by Council member Christopher Marte, notably doesn't require the creation of such programs or earmark a specific amount of money for that purpose, one of several reasons Samuelsen cited in lampooning the bill. "It only says the city should prepare a worker transition plan by April 2027 and include weak measures like job fairs and job counseling. It says the city should 'consider' financial compensation for carriage owners who spent hundreds of thousands of dollars to buy city-issued medallions and build up their businesses," the union head's statement said. According to Menin's office, the speaker will convene a working group focused on addressing any issues that come up during the industry's phase-out period. The speaker will invite the TWU and the mayor's administration to participate in that process. On the other end of the debate, the finalized version of the bill requires carriage horse owners who want to sell their animals to do so in a "humane manner." "A licensed horse may not be sold or otherwise transferred to a person for purposes of slaughter, resale for slaughter, or holding or transport for slaughter, or for use in a horse drawn cab business," a new paragraph inserted into the bill says. The legislation notes that all licensed carriage horse owners must by March 1, 2027, certify to the city that they won't violate the sales restrictions. "This legislation means so much to those who have spent years fighting with us to protect horses and prevent tragedy," said Steve Nislick, co-founding president of New Yorkers for Clean, Livable and Safe Streets, one of the main groups pushing for a carriage ban. "Thanks to Speaker Menin's fortitude and compassion, New York City is finally poised to close this painful chapter." The latest incarnation of the bill began to gain serious momentum over the summer after Romanch Mahajan, an 18-year-old Indian tourist, died when he jumped off a carriage to try to save his mom, who had been flung off the buggy when the horse unexpectedly careened into a gallop. Though many horses have perished in carriage accidents over the years, Mahajan is believed to have been the first human to die in such an accident in modern times. After his death, the bill was renamed "Romanch's Law." The first serious effort to outlaw the city's carriage industry came in 2010, when then-Council Speaker Melissa Mark-Viverito introduced a bill to replace the horse-drawn carriages with electric vehicles. After that bill died during former Mayor Michael Bloomberg's tenure, Bill de Blasio promised as part of his successful 2013 mayoral campaign to enact a ban — but he never made good on that pledge. Former Mayor Eric Adams then also tried to outlaw the carriages in the final months of his term last year. But he too fell short amid resistance from the TWU and Council members aligned with the union. The robot is able to process speech and vision through onboard AI and can have its actions pre-programmed or be manually operated with a remote control.
